stem:
The elements in Group 17, the halogens, and their compounds, show many similarities and trends in their properties. Some data are given for the elements fluorine to iodine.

| element | bond energy /$\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ | standard enthalpy change of atomisation, $\Delta H_{\text{at}}^{\ominus}$/$\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ | boiling point of element /$\text{K}$ | boiling point of **hydrogen halide** /$\text{K}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| fluorine, $\text{F}-\text{F}$ | 158 | 79 | 85 | 293 |
| chlorine, $\text{Cl}-\text{Cl}$ | 242 | 121 | 238 | 188 |
| bromine, $\text{Br}-\text{Br}$ | 193 | 112 | 332 | 206 |
| iodine, $\text{I}-\text{I}$ | 151 | 107 | 457 | 238 |

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Explain the meaning of the term *standard enthalpy change of atomisation*.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
For fluorine and chlorine, the enthalpy changes of atomisation are half the value of the bond energies.

For bromine and iodine, the enthalpy changes of atomisation are much more than half the value of the bond energies.

Suggest a reason for this difference.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text:
The standard enthalpy of formation of iodine monochloride, $\text{ICl}$, is $-24.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Use this information and the bond energies of iodine and chlorine to calculate the $\text{I}-\text{Cl}$ bond energy.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain the trend in the boiling points of the hydrogen halides, $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest why the hydrogen halide HF does not follow the trend in boiling points shown by $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem:
In an experiment, two of the halogens are represented as $\mathbf{P}_2$ and $\mathbf{Q}_2$.

$\mathbf{P}_2$ combines with hydrogen on heating to form $\text{H}\mathbf{P}$, which can be easily broken down into its elements. A solution of $\text{H}\mathbf{P}$ in water reacts with aqueous silver ions to form a yellow precipitate that is insoluble in dilute aqueous ammonia.

$\mathbf{Q}_2$ combines explosively with hydrogen in sunlight to form $\text{H}\mathbf{Q}$, which is stable to heat. A solution of $\text{H}\mathbf{Q}$ in water reacts with aqueous silver ions to form a white precipitate that is soluble in dilute aqueous ammonia.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: $\text{H}\mathbf{P}$ readily decomposes into its elements when heated but $\text{H}\mathbf{Q}$ is stable to heat. Explain this with reference to bond energies.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: Write an equation for the thermal decomposition of $\text{H}\mathbf{P}$.

parts.label: (c)(iv)
parts.text:
Write ionic equations, including state symbols, for

1. the formation of the white precipitate on addition of aqueous silver ions to aqueous $\text{H}\mathbf{Q}$,

2. the subsequent dissolving of this precipitate in dilute aqueous ammonia.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Chlorine reacts directly with many elements to form chlorides. Three such compounds are $\text{MgCl}_2$, $\text{AlCl}_3$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.text: State and explain the pattern shown by the formulae of these three chlorides.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text: Write equations to show the behaviour of each of these chlorides when added to water.
